title: Aria's Fuzzy Shadows
markdown:
The fire crackled in Gran Ruth’s hearth, orange glow dancing across the cozy cottage. A woolly sock in progress sat in the basket like a second, quieter fire. Aria, pigtails bobbing with every wiggle, tried to show Miso the mouse a shadow puppet she had practised on the walk over. She wiggled fingers in front of the table lamp. The wall got a big blurry smudge, a grey cloud that had forgotten its edges and any claim to being a frog.

“Oh dear!” Miso giggled, whiskers twitching so hard his nose wiggled. “A soaring eagle? Or a fluffy cloud with a very bad hair day?”

Aria giggled too, then a ladybug-sized frown. “A leaping frog. Excited. Jumpy. It’s fuzzy. Wobbly jelly.”

Ruth, knitting a sunflower-yellow sock, peered over her spectacles. Needles clicked. “Shadows can be shy. Hide-and-seek with their shapes.”

Aria tried something new. Delicate seeds needed close attention; maybe fingers did too. She moved her hands toward the lamp, inch by inch. The smudge shrank. Sharper. Closer still, right by the warm glow: tiny and crisp, a bakery cookie. “Smaller and clearer when I’m close.”

“Look!” A frog, almost ready to hop.

Miso scampered, beady eyes on the wall. “When your hands are far, a wobbly blob that might float away.”

The frown left. She experimented: far — big blurry pudding; closer — shrink and sharpen; away — a fuzzy giant. A game of big-and-small.

“Close to the light: small and neat. Far: big and messy, like spilled juice.”

Ruth’s needles kept time. She named the rule without my-clever or hidden secrets: close to the light, sharp shadow; further, the light spreads, bigger, fuzzier — ripples on a pond, if you needed a picture.

They spent the evening on a shadow zoo: tiny sharp mouse, clearer cat, a grand bird with wings that looked ready to leave the wall. Aria made a crisp seed, like the ones she collected.

“Distance between the light and the hand?” Miso nudged a pebble, as if testing.

“Precisely.” Ruth nodded. Light as artist; distance as brush. She stopped there.

Aria coiled the lamp cord so it would not tug the table and spoil the next frog. Miso sat in the smallest sharp shadow he could find, which was, for a mouse, a kind of compliment.
